summary: RPL uses Objective Functions to decide how nodes select and optimize routes. This RFC specifies Objective Function Zero, a basic one that works with the default RPL framework and does not need particular metrics.

plainLanguage.summary: RPL needs a rule for choosing among paths. This is the simple everyday rule that picks a good parent without fancy measurements.

questions: how does rpl choose a parent
what is rpl objective function zero
subtitle: The simple default rule RPL nodes use to pick a parent and compute their Rank, so different implementations can interoperate.

tldr.problem: RPL leaves the choice of routes to a pluggable Objective Function but defines none, so two implementations might share no Objective Function and fail to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Objective Function Zero (OF0) sets a node's Rank to its preferred parent's Rank plus a bounded, positive rank_increase, and picks a preferred parent and a backup feasible successor by an ordered list of rules.
tldr.outcome: OF0 is a basic Objective Function that uses only objects defined in RPL, needs no metric containers, and has Objective Code Point 0. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6552 is a Proposed Standard from March 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It was published alongside RFC 6550, the RPL specification it builds on.

sections.title: Why RPL Needs a Default Objective Function
sections.content:
The Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL, RFC 6550) is a generic distance vector protocol. It is adapted to different network types by plugging in an Objective Function (OF). An OF states the outcome of the process a node uses to select and optimize routes. The RFC stresses that an OF is not an algorithm: outside RPL, "shortest path first" is an OF, and Dijkstra is one algorithm that can satisfy it.

RPL itself defines no OF and no default metric container. The RFC points out the risk: unless two implementations follow the same guidance, they might not support a common OF and so could not interoperate. Objective Function Zero (OF0) is designed as a default OF that lets implementations interoperate across a wide range of use cases.

To make that possible, OF0 does not say how link properties are turned into a number. It leaves that to the implementation, but it fixes the allowed range of the result. It also ignores metric containers. RPL requires all nodes in a network to use a common OF; using several OFs in one network is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: RPL says nodes must follow some rule to choose a path, but it never says which rule. OF0 is a basic rule everyone can agree on if they have nothing better.

sections.title: What OF0 Aims For
sections.content:
The goal of OF0 is for a node to join a DODAG Version that offers good enough connectivity to a specific set of nodes or to a larger routing infrastructure. There is no guarantee that the path is optimal for any specific metric. How that connectivity is checked depends on the implementation and link type and is out of scope. For OF0, a Grounded DODAG simply means the root provides such connectivity.

OF0 tries to find the nearest Grounded root. That works when a node's Rank is close to an abstract function of its distance to the root. This is balanced against keeping some path diversity, which can be achieved by increasing the Rank. With no Grounded root, floating DAGs form, rooted at the nodes with the highest administrative preference.

A node selects one preferred parent and, if one is available, a backup feasible successor. Upward traffic normally goes through the preferred parent, with no attempt at load balancing. When link conditions do not let a packet through the preferred parent, the packet is passed to the backup.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kid walks toward the teacher through one favorite neighbor. If that neighbor is busy, the kid uses a spare neighbor instead.

sections.title: Computing Rank
sections.content:
A node's Rank is an abstract distance to the root. In OF0 it is the preferred parent's Rank plus a strictly positive rank_increase, so Rank always increases away from the root and, after convergence, paths are loop-free.

The implementation first computes a step_of_rank (Sp) for each candidate parent from link properties. The RFC does not prescribe the formula, but normalizes the range: from 1 (excellent) to 9 (worst acceptable). Basing it on a static metric such as administrative cost gives a Rank like hop count, which tends to favor fewer but longer, poorer hops, so the RFC RECOMMENDS using dynamic properties such as the expected transmission count (ETX).

Two optional knobs adjust the result. The rank_factor (Rf) multiplies the effect of link properties so that, for example, powered or wired links can be favored over battery or wireless ones. The stretch_of_rank (Sr) can widen a step to allow a feasible successor to be selected, but stretching is NOT RECOMMENDED because it distorts the DODAG and can cause instability when nodes raise their Ranks to use each other as parents.

The result is expressed in units of MinHopRankIncrease, which defaults to DEFAULT_MIN_HOP_RANK_INCREASE from RFC 6550. With that default the least significant octet of the Rank field in the DIO Base Object is not used.

By default OF0 encodes the 2-octet Rank in units of 256. The default settings allow a minimum of 28 hops (worst acceptable) and a maximum of 255 hops (excellent).
sections.plainLanguage: Your score is your parent's score plus the cost of the hop to them. Bad hops cost more, good hops cost less, and the cost can never be zero, so scores always grow as you walk away from the leader.

sections.title: Variables, Parameters and Constants
sections.content:
OF0 adds two variables, step_of_rank and rank_increase, both strictly positive integers. It also defines two optional configurable parameters. stretch_of_rank is the maximum added to a step; if none is configured, no stretching happens. rank_factor is a strictly positive integer; if none is configured, 1 is used.

The implementation MUST keep the stretched step between the minimum and maximum step constants, and MUST set rank_factor between its minimum and maximum. OF0 fixes the following constants:

  • DEFAULT_STEP_OF_RANK: 3
  • MINIMUM_STEP_OF_RANK: 1 and MAXIMUM_STEP_OF_RANK: 9
  • DEFAULT_RANK_STRETCH: 0 and MAXIMUM_RANK_STRETCH: 5
  • DEFAULT_RANK_FACTOR: 1, MINIMUM_RANK_FACTOR: 1 and MAXIMUM_RANK_FACTOR: 4

An implementation SHOULD allow at least a global rank_factor to be configured, and MAY allow a maximum stretch_of_rank, which MUST NOT exceed MAXIMUM_RANK_STRETCH. At factory time the default constants SHOULD be used. Changed values apply at the next Version of the DODAG.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook sets the lowest and highest cost a hop can have, so nobody can cheat by making a hop look free or impossibly expensive.

sections.title: Choosing Parents
sections.content:
As OF0 scans candidate neighbors, it keeps the best one by an ordered list of criteria. The first is a hard rule: a candidate that would break the re-parenting rules of RFC 6550, Section 8, MUST NOT be considered. After that come preferences, mostly SHOULD-level, such as:

  • a router that passed a connectivity and suitability check over one that did not;
  • a router on a higher-order interface when a local interface policy exists;
  • a router offering connectivity to a Grounded DODAG Version, or to a more preferable root;
  • a router on the most recent DODAG Version of the same DODAG;
  • the parent giving the lesser resulting Rank;
  • the parent already in use, then the one that announced a DIO message more recently.

There is also an optional check that prefers a DODAG Version for which an alternate parent exists.

For the backup feasible successor, the node MUST NOT pick the preferred parent, and the candidate MUST be in the same or a subsequent DODAG Version. A router in the same Version with a Rank higher than the Rank computed for this node MUST NOT be selected. Then a lesser Rank, a validated router, a higher-order interface and the one already in use are preferred. For both lists, an implementation MAY vary the rules and their order according to configured policy.
sections.plainLanguage: To choose a neighbor to follow, you check a list: is it allowed, does it really connect to the leader, is it up to date, and is it close. Pick the winner, and keep a runner-up in case the winner trips.

sections.title: Interface, Management and IANA
sections.content:
OF0 talks to the RPL core in four ways. When a DIO is received, the OF matching its Objective Code Point (OCP) is run, and OF0 is OCP 0. OF0 can return DAG information (DIO base header material, the node's role and Rank), return the ordered list of parents and feasible successors, and raise events when DAG information or the parent list changes, which may cause the RPL core to send a new DIO or reset Trickle timers.

For manageability, OF0 inherits RPL's management, except that the metrics of RFC 6551 are not used and need no management. An implementation SHOULD support the DODAG Configuration option, which can distribute MinHopRankIncrease and override the default fixed value of 256. For monitoring, it should expose DAG information (DODAGID, RPLInstanceID, Mode of Operation, Rank, Version Number, Grounded flag) and a neighbor list with the preferred parent and any alternate.

IANA assigned OCP code 0 in the Objective Code Point Registry, described as a basic Objective Function that relies only on the objects defined in RFC 6550, with RFC 6552 as the defining RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: OF0 has a label, number zero, so a node can tell which rulebook is being used. It also has a few dials and gauges so a person can set and check it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OF0 makes simple extensions to RPL and adds no new flows or messages, so it needs no specific new mitigation and inherits the threats and mechanisms of RFC 6550 and the ROLL security framework.

OF0 depends on information in the Rank and OCP protocol elements. If those were compromised, an implementation might generate the wrong path for a packet and misroute it. Deployments are therefore RECOMMENDED to use RPL security mechanisms when routing information might be modified or spoofed.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone lies about their score, kids could follow the wrong neighbor and get lost. So where lying is possible, use the locks RPL provides.
